newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Cambodia's Ranariddh meets Indonesia's Suharto.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Ranariddh meets Indonesia's Suharto.

text.p: Cambodia's ousted premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh visited Jakarta on Wednesday for a closed-door meeting with President Suharto as the government of the rival who overthrew him asked for Southeast Asian mediation in their dispute.
Ranariddh, who was overthrown by co-Prime Minister Hun Sen in a bloody putsch earlier this month, flew into Jakarta on a commercial flight from Singapore, foreign ministry officials said.

He avoided reporters at the airport, flying into the city in a helicopter, and held a 40-minute meeting with Suharto at his private residence after slipping out of the luxury hotel where he was staying through a side entrance.
"I had a good meeting with President Suharto. I came to thank him," Ranariddh told reporters on his return from the president's house before disappearing into his suite.
Plainclothes Indonesian bodyguards blocked reporters from following him. Reporters were also kept at a distance from Suharto's residence.

Ranariddh's visit coincided with a meeting in Kuala Lumpur of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) at which Cambodia's neighbours rejected a last-minute plea by the Hun Sen government to join the regional grouping.
Ranariddh had said in Singapore on Monday that he planned to visit Indonesia.
Jakarta was co-chair of the 1991 Paris talks that ended decades of bloodshed in Cambodia and laid the ground for United Nations-sponsored elections in 1993.

Ranariddh won the poll and agreed to an uneasy power-sharing coalition with Hun Sen as so-called second prime minister -- a merger that crumbled earlier this month when Hun Sen's forces ousted royalist troops loyal to Ranariddh in a coup.

ASEAN held a special ceremony in Kuala Lumpur on Wednesday to welcome new members Burma and Laos but opted to continue to postpone Cambodia's membership indefinitely. Other members include Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot, who has been named to replace Ranariddh as first prime minister, told reporters in Kuala Lumpur earlier in the day that Phnom Penh wanted to reverse its previous hardline stance and join ASEAN, asking it to mediate in the conflict between the warring prime ministers.
But Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi said: "We feel there is still instability in Cambodia and we reaffirmed our decision not to induct Cambodia on the 23rd."
Asian diplomats in Phnom Penh welcomed the Cambodian government's apparent about-face on mediation but said they were waiting to hear Hun Sen announce the policy himself.
Diplomatic sources in Jakarta said Ranariddh would leave for Bangkok on Thursday where he will meet U.S. President Bill Clinton's special envoy, former congressman Stephen Solarz.
Solarz, who is on an Asian trip to help find a solution to the Cambodian imbroglio, held a meeting with Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas in Kuala Lumpur on Wednesday.
"We very much want to work with our friends in ASEAN and other countries in the region," Solarz told reporters after the meeting.
